articleHeadline: Child with high fever and sore throat, refusing to eat: beware of herpangina.
articleSummary: Herpangina is an acute enterovirus infection primarily affecting children under six, per Fujian Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Transmission occurs via fecal-oral, respiratory droplets, and direct contact, with outbreaks common in nurseries and kindergartens. Sudden fever (39–41°C) peaks within 24–48 hours, followed by sore throat and pharyngeal redness with scattered gray-white vesicles (1–2 mm) around a red halo; these vesicles rupture to yellow ulcers within 2–3 days. Young children may refuse meals, drool, and be irritable; swallowing is painful. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive: antipyretics, cooling, fluids, and soft, cool foods, plus mouth care. The illness is usually self-limiting within about a week; rare cases progress to persistent fever, rapid breathing, somnolence, or tremors requiring medical care. Prevention emphasizes handwashing, reduced gatherings, disinfection, and morning screening in childcare settings.

articleSummary: PM2.5 exposure is linked to higher risk of Influenza A infection in humans. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis across 16 studies reports that every 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 correlates with about a 1.5% rise in influenza risk, as ultrafine particles penetrate deep into the respiratory tract. NHLBI-funded research suggests pollutants can accumulate in pulmonary lymph nodes, potentially disrupting immune cell function and raising susceptibility. WHO identifies air pollution as a major driver of acute and chronic respiratory disease, with NO2 and ozone also threats. CDC recommends annual vaccination, hand hygiene, and indoor air quality; mitigation includes monitoring air quality and using protective masks in high-pollution areas.

articleHeadline: Aurora intensifies drive against ASF
articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) in Maria Aurora, Aurora province triggers intensified controls. The municipal government warns barangay officials against trading live pigs or pork products, with sanctions for tolerance. More than 90.2 kg of frozen and processed pork were confiscated and destroyed at the market as part of the ASF response. In Barangay Baubo, 182 pigs were culled on Sept. 23, 2026, by the Municipal Agriculture Office, the Provincial Veterinary Office of Aurora, and DA Regional Field Office 3. Officials say the virus can persist in contaminated meat and spread through transport of animals and pork products, so monitoring of farms, markets, transport routes, and quarantine and inspection protocols is enforced. Compensation under the ASF program ranges from 90% of pig value for registered farmers to 20% for unregistered backyard raisers. Registration is urged to access full assistance; movement restrictions and biosecurity measures remain in force with ongoing monitoring.

articleHeadline: BDRCS, IFRC scale up dengue response to reach 300,000 people
articleSummary: Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS), with IFRC support, is scaling a six‑month dengue response to reach about 300,000 people—prioritizing high‑transmission communities and vulnerable families. The effort follows sharp dengue rises after late August’s heavy monsoon rains. As of Sept 23, 67,367 dengue patients had been hospitalised and 201 deaths, up from 43,173 hospitalised and 184 deaths during the same period in 2025; eight more fatalities and 1,782 hospitalisations were reported in the 24 hours to 8:00 am on Thursday, raising 2026’s toll to 209. The operation covers Dhaka, Khulna, Barishal, Chattogram, and camps for displaced people from Rakhine State and host communities in Cox’s Bazar, with possible expansion. Funded by IFRC’s DREF, it mobilises 1,000 volunteers, provides 100,000 IV saline units, 50,000 dengue test kits, 3,000 triple blood bags, 100 apheresis kits, 2,500 mosquito nets, and BDT 10,000 one‑time cash to 2,500 vulnerable households, plus training for 150 health professionals.

articleHeadline: Anthrax suspected in 46 hippo deaths in Zambia amid potential spillover to humans
articleSummary: Anthrax outbreak in Muchinga, northern Zambia, linked to hippos with 46 hippo deaths since Aug. 31; anthrax laboratory-confirmed in one hippo. Five buffalo carcasses tested negative; ten elephants under investigation, none lab-confirmed. As of Sept. 21, 21 people were suspected of contracting Bacillus anthracis in Muchinga; only one laboratory-confirmed human case; no deaths reported at that time. Immediate concern centers on wildlife–livestock–human interface, carcass contamination, and exposure risk from handling or consuming meat of animals found dead. Sept. 10 advisory from the Disaster Risk Management Division urges avoiding meat from animals that may have died from anthrax and reporting suspected carcasses to authorities. A national vaccination campaign is underway alongside intensified wildlife and livestock surveillance and laboratory testing. In 2023, four people died and more were infected across nine of Zambia’s ten provinces, highlighting spillover risks and the need for community reporting and vaccination.
notes: 2023年には同国内で炭疽病により4名が死亡した既往があり、今回も21名がBacillus anthracis感染疑いで確認済みは1名（死亡例なし）。国家ワクチン接種キャンペーンとサーベイランス強化が進行中。続報でヒト症例の重症度・拡大状況を確認する必要あり。
